title: Normalization & Transaction Management
intro: Normal forms, transactions, concurrency, deadlocks and crash recovery.

sec.s: A database management system (DBMS) stores and manages data in a structured way.

b.x: A database management system (DBMS) stores and manages data in a structured way. A well-designed database should avoid unnecessary duplication, preserve correct relationships among records, support multiple users safely, and recover correctly after failures.
Normalization and transaction management solve two related but different classes of problems.

Normalization is a database-design technique. It organizes tables and their relationships so that redundant data is reduced and insertion, update, and deletion anomalies are avoided. Functional dependencies are used to reason about which attributes determine other attributes. Normal forms such as 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, and BCNF provide progressively stronger rules for structuring relational tables.

Transaction management concerns the safe execution of database operations. A transaction may involve one SQL statement or a sequence of statements that must be treated as one logical unit. Transaction management helps ensure that operations remain correct even when multiple users work at the same time or a system fails unexpectedly.

For example, suppose a student pays a college fee. The system might need to decrease the student's outstanding balance and record the payment. If only one of those changes is saved, the database may become inconsistent. A transaction groups the related changes together so that either all required changes are committed or the incomplete work is rolled back.

Similarly, suppose a college stores a student's department name repeatedly in every course-enrolment row. A department rename could require updating many rows. If some rows are missed, contradictory department names appear. Normalization helps place department information in an appropriate table and connect it using keys.
The major learning goals of this topic are

x: Understand functional dependencies and attribute keys.
Identify anomalies caused by poor table design.
Understand lossless decomposition and dependency preservation.
Explain transactions and the ACID properties.
Understand concurrency problems and locking protocols.
Explain deadlocks and their handling techniques.
Describe basic crash-recovery mechanisms such as logs, checkpoints, undo, and redo.

sec.s: A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between attributes in a relational table.

b.x: A functional dependency (FD) is a constraint between attributes in a relational table. It states that the value of one attribute, or a group of attributes, uniquely determines the value of another attribute or group of attributes.
Read this as “X functionally determines Y.”
Here, X and Y are sets of attributes. If two rows have the same values for all attributes in X, they must also have the same values for all attributes in Y.
If each StudentID belongs to exactly one student, then:
These dependencies say that knowing the StudentID is enough to determine the student's name, email, and department, assuming the design rules guarantee one current value for each.

An FD is a rule about all valid states of the database, not merely a pattern noticed in the rows currently stored. If the current sample happens to have unique names, that does not automatically mean StudentName determines StudentID. Two students may share the same name in a future valid database state.

x: Y is called the dependent attribute set.

b.x: For StudentID → StudentName, StudentID is the determinant and StudentName is the dependent attribute.
A functional dependency X → Y is trivial when Y is a subset of X.
These dependencies are always true because the right-hand attributes are already included in the left-hand side.
An FD is non-trivial when Y is not a subset of X.
A dependency is completely non-trivial if X and Y have no attributes in common.
Y is fully functionally dependent on X when X determines Y, but no proper subset of X can determine Y.
Consider ENROLMENT(StudentID, CourseID, Grade), where a student can take multiple courses and each student-course pair has one grade.
If neither StudentID alone nor CourseID alone determines Grade, then Grade is fully dependent on the composite key (StudentID, CourseID).
A partial dependency occurs when a non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key.
Assume the candidate key is (StudentID, CourseID).

StudentName depends on only StudentID, which is part of the composite key. CourseName depends on only CourseID. These are partial dependencies and cause a violation of 2NF when the relevant dependent attributes are non-prime.
A transitive dependency occurs when X determines Y and Y determines Z, so X also determines Z through Y.
If DepartmentName is stored in the STUDENT table, it is transitively dependent on StudentID through DepartmentID. This can cause a 3NF violation, depending on keys and the complete dependency set.
A superkey is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies each row in a relation. It may contain unnecessary attributes.
A candidate key is a minimal superkey: it uniquely identifies rows, and no proper subset of it does so.

If both StudentID and Email are unique and neither can be null under the business rules, then {StudentID} and {Email} may both be candidate keys. {StudentID, Email} is a superkey but not a candidate key because StudentID alone is enough.
A primary key is the candidate key selected as the main identifier. Other candidate keys are often called alternate keys.
A prime attribute is an attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key.
A non-prime attribute does not belong to any candidate key.
This distinction is especially important for 3NF. The phrase “prime attribute” does not mean an attribute is important in ordinary language; it is a technical term based on candidate keys.
Armstrong's axioms are inference rules used to derive functional dependencies logically implied by a given set of FDs.

x: If Y is a subset of X, then X → Y.

b.x: If X → Y, then XZ → YZ for any attribute set Z.

x: If X → Y and Y → Z, then X → Z.
If X → Y and X → Z, then X → YZ.
If X → YZ, then X → Y and X → Z.
If X → Y and WY → Z, then WX → Z.

b.x: These rules help determine keys, reason about normal forms, and test whether a dependency follows from another set of dependencies.
The closure of an attribute set X, written X+, is the set of all attributes that can be functionally determined by X using the given FDs.

x: If A is contained in the current closure, add B.
Repeat until no more attributes can be added.
Relation R(A, B, C, D), with:
A → B, so add B: {A, B}
B → C, so add C: {A, B, C}
AC → D applies because A and C are now present, so add D.

b.x: Therefore A is a superkey. If A is a single attribute and no smaller proper subset exists, it is a candidate key.

x: Determine whether a table satisfies a normal form.

b.x: Remember: dependencies come from the meaning and rules of the data. They should not be guessed solely from a small sample of rows.

sec.t: Database Anomalies and the Need for Normalization
sec.s: Normalization organizes relations to reduce avoidable redundancy and anomalies.

b.x: Normalization organizes relations to reduce avoidable redundancy and anomalies.

x: StudentID | StudentName | CourseID | CourseName | InstructorName | Grade
101       | Asha        | C1       | DBMS       | Mr. Rao        | A
101       | Asha        | C2       | Python     | Ms. Sen        | B
102       | Kabir       | C1       | DBMS       | Mr. Rao        | A-
103       | Meera       | C1       | DBMS       | Mr. Rao        | B+

b.x: The student name repeats for every course taken by that student. CourseName and InstructorName repeat for each enrolment in the same course.
If the DBMS course changes its name, every row containing that course may need an update. If one row is missed, the database contains conflicting course names.
Normalization places course information in one COURSE row, so the course name can be updated once.

Suppose a new course is created before any student enrols in it. If the only place to store course details is ENROLMENT, the database may be unable to store the course without inventing a student-enrolment record.
Separating COURSE from ENROLMENT permits the course to be inserted independently.

Suppose the last student enrolled in a course is removed from ENROLMENT. If the course name and instructor are stored only in that row, deleting it also removes the only stored information about the course.
A separate COURSE table prevents this unintended loss.
3.4 Normalization does not mean eliminating every repeated value

Repeated foreign-key values are often necessary. For example, many enrolment rows may contain the same CourseID. That repetition is not necessarily a design defect; it represents relationships between students and courses.
The aim is to avoid storing the same fact in multiple places where it can become inconsistent. Normalization should preserve the meaning of the data while structuring dependencies correctly.

sec.s: A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) when each attribute value is atomic within the chosen relational…

b.x: A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) when each attribute value is atomic within the chosen relational model and each row-column intersection contains a single value rather than a repeating group or list of values.
In introductory database courses, 1NF is usually explained as:

x: There are no lists or repeating groups inside a single field.
Values in a column come from the same defined domain.

b.x: “Atomic” depends partly on the intended data model. For example, a phone number may be stored as a single text value if the application treats it as one value, even though its characters could be split. Atomicity means the value is not being used as an unstructured list of separate items in that relation.
PhoneNumbers contains a list in one cell. This makes it difficult to search for one number, validate individual numbers, or join phone numbers to other data.
Option A: One phone number per student row:
This can satisfy 1NF, but student information is repeated.
A suitable key for STUDENT_PHONE may be (StudentID, PhoneNumber), assuming a student cannot have duplicate entries for the same number.

A table with columns Phone1, Phone2, Phone3, and so on may also represent a repeating group. Such a design limits the number of values and complicates queries. A separate child table is often more flexible.

x: It makes each value easier to query and validate.
It supports relational operations more consistently.
It avoids hidden lists inside cells.
It gives later normalization rules a useful foundation.

b.x: 1NF alone does not eliminate all redundancy. A table can satisfy 1NF and still have partial or transitive dependencies.

sec.s: For many introductory examples, the focus is on a composite candidate key.

b.x: A relation is in Second Normal Form (2NF) if

x: Every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key; equivalently, there is no partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on a proper subset of a candidate key.

b.x: For many introductory examples, the focus is on a composite candidate key. If the only candidate key has a single attribute, partial dependency on part of that key cannot occur, so a 1NF relation with only single-attribute candidate keys is in 2NF.
Be careful: the formal rule considers all candidate keys, not only the primary key chosen by the designer.
StudentName depends only on StudentID, and CourseName depends only on CourseID. Both depend on part of the composite key, not the entire key. Therefore, the relation violates 2NF.
The student's name is stored once in STUDENT. The course name is stored once in COURSE. The grade depends on the combination of student and course, so it remains in ENROLMENT.
If a student's name changes, one row in STUDENT is updated. If a course name changes, one row in COURSE is updated. Enrolment rows retain the relationship and grade.

x: Check whether any non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of any candidate key.
If such a partial dependency exists, decompose the relation while preserving its meaning and relationships.
a relation is not automatically in 2NF just because its primary key is declared as a composite key. You must examine the functional dependencies.

sec.s: A relation is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → A, at least…

b.x: A relation is in Third Normal Form (3NF) if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → A, at least one of these conditions holds:

The rule is applied to dependencies implied by the relation's constraints. In many introductory explanations, 3NF is described as being in 2NF with no inappropriate transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on a key. That explanation is useful for common examples, while the formal definition above handles more general cases.

StudentID is the key. DepartmentName is determined by DepartmentID, which is determined by StudentID. If DepartmentName is stored in STUDENT, it is transitively dependent on StudentID through DepartmentID.
The dependency DepartmentID → DepartmentName violates 3NF in this relation if DepartmentID is not a superkey and DepartmentName is non-prime.

x: StudentID determines StudentName and DepartmentID in STUDENT.
Student records refer to departments through DepartmentID.
Prevents inconsistent updates to facts about departments, instructors, or other entities.
Avoids many insertion and deletion anomalies.
Usually gives a practical balance between good structure and efficient queries.
Often allows a decomposition that preserves dependencies.

b.x: The formal definition of 3NF allows a dependency X → A when A is a prime attribute even if X is not a superkey. This exception is important and distinguishes 3NF from BCNF.

x: R(A, B, C), with candidate keys AB and AC, and dependency B → C.

Here C is prime because it belongs to candidate key AC. B is not a superkey. The dependency can satisfy the 3NF condition because the right-hand attribute C is prime, but it violates BCNF because B is not a superkey.
Examine each non-trivial FD X → A.
Check whether X is a superkey.
If X is not a superkey, check whether A is prime.
If neither condition holds, the relation violates 3NF.

b.x: Do not rely only on the phrase “remove transitive dependencies.” It is a useful memory aid but the formal test is more reliable.

sec.s: A relation is in Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y that…

b.x: A relation is in Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y that holds in the relation, X is a superkey.
In simple terms, every determinant of a non-trivial functional dependency must be a superkey.
BCNF is stricter than 3NF because it does not include the 3NF exception for a prime attribute on the right-hand side.
A relation can satisfy 3NF but still contain redundancy caused by a determinant that is not a superkey. BCNF removes this particular pattern.
7.3 Example of a relation in 3NF but not BCNF

x: A student can enrol in many courses.
Each course can have multiple instructors.
Each instructor teaches exactly one course in this simplified example.
An instructor's course is therefore determined by Instructor.

b.x: Assume the candidate keys are (Student, Course) and (Student, Instructor). This is because either pair determines the remaining attribute under the stated dependencies.
The dependency Instructor → Course has a determinant Instructor that is not a superkey. So it violates BCNF.
Course is a prime attribute because it belongs to candidate key (Student, Course). Thus the dependency can satisfy 3NF's prime-attribute exception while violating BCNF.
Decompose R(Student, Course, Instructor) using Instructor → Course into:

The first table records the course assigned to an instructor. The second records which instructors teach which students. The exact interpretation of this decomposition depends on the business rules. In a real schema, confirm that it preserves all required semantics and does not introduce spurious combinations.

x: Find a non-trivial FD X → Y that violates BCNF, meaning X is not a superkey.
Repeat the process on resulting relations until every relation satisfies BCNF.

b.x: A standard BCNF decomposition based on a violating FD is lossless, but BCNF decomposition does not always preserve every original functional dependency in a way that can be enforced locally. This trade-off is important.

x: Removes more FD-based redundancy than 3NF in cases where 3NF permits a non-superkey determinant.
Helps prevent anomalies arising from those dependencies.
It may not preserve all functional dependencies after decomposition.
Enforcing some constraints may require joins or additional mechanisms.
More tables can mean more joins in queries.

b.x: A practical design may choose 3NF when dependency preservation is particularly important, or BCNF when eliminating the relevant redundancy is the priority and the constraints can still be enforced reliably.

sec.s: The slogan “the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key” is a simplified memory aid often used for…

x: Each cell contains one value under the chosen relational model.
No repeating groups or lists of independent values inside a field.
Does not by itself remove partial or transitive dependencies.
Every non-prime attribute must depend on the whole of every candidate key.
Removes partial dependencies on a proper subset of a candidate key.
Must satisfy 2NF in the usual progression of normalization.
Formal rule: for every non-trivial FD X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime.
For every non-trivial FD X → Y, X must be a superkey.
3NF: nothing but the key should determine non-prime descriptive facts, subject to the formal 3NF rule.
BCNF: every determinant must be a superkey.

b.x: The slogan “the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key” is a simplified memory aid often used for 1NF/2NF/3NF. It is not a complete substitute for the formal definitions, especially when there are multiple candidate keys.

sec.t: Decomposition: Lossless Join and Dependency Preservation
sec.s: Normalization often splits one relation into multiple relations.

b.x: Normalization often splits one relation into multiple relations. A good decomposition should preserve the ability to reconstruct the original information and, where possible, enforce the original dependencies without expensive joins.
Decomposition means replacing a relation R with two or more smaller relations whose attributes collectively represent R.

A decomposition is lossless if joining the decomposed relations reconstructs exactly the original relation for every valid database state. It must not create extra rows that were not present in the original information.

For a binary decomposition of R into R1 and R2, a standard lossless-join test under functional dependencies is that the common attributes R1 intersect R2 functionally determine all attributes of at least one of the two relations, according to the dependencies relevant to R.
the common attribute is DepartmentID. If DepartmentID is a key of DEPARTMENT, joining STUDENT with DEPARTMENT on DepartmentID correctly attaches one department name to each student row.
A decomposition is lossy if joining the resulting tables can create spurious tuples, or combinations that were not valid in the original relation.
If it is split carelessly into AB and BC tables, joining them on B1 may produce combinations not present originally. Such spurious rows are evidence of a lossy decomposition.
A decomposition is dependency-preserving if all original functional dependencies can be enforced by checking constraints on the decomposed relations individually, without needing to join them.
Dependency preservation is valuable because it makes validation simpler and often more efficient.

x: Lossless join concerns whether the original data can be reconstructed correctly.
Dependency preservation concerns whether the original constraints can be enforced locally.

b.x: A decomposition can be lossless but fail to preserve every functional dependency. BCNF decompositions can have this issue. A well-designed 3NF synthesis can produce a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition under the standard algorithm and assumptions.

sec.s: A transaction is a sequence of database operations treated as one logical unit of work.

b.x: A transaction is a sequence of database operations treated as one logical unit of work. The transaction may read data, insert records, update values, or delete records.

x: transferring ₹500 from account A to account B.

b.x: If the database subtracts ₹500 from A but fails before adding it to B, the transfer is incomplete. Transaction management is designed to prevent the database from permanently accepting this partial result.

x: BEGIN or START TRANSACTION begins a transaction.
COMMIT makes its changes permanent according to the system's transaction guarantees.
ROLLBACK cancels uncommitted changes in the transaction.

b.x: Exact syntax and behavior vary by DBMS. Some systems automatically start transactions; some statements may cause implicit commits; and certain DDL operations behave differently across systems.

If a required step fails before commit, the application should roll back the transaction. In real financial code, validate the sender's balance, account identities, currency, and other business rules, and check that each statement affects the expected rows.

A DBMS may serve many users at once. One transaction may update an account while another reads it. A power failure may happen after some data pages are written but before all changes are complete. A transaction system must manage these cases.

x: Treat related operations as a unit.
Prevent incomplete work from corrupting the database's logical state.

sec.s: ACID is a set of four important properties used to describe reliable transaction processing: Atomicity,…

b.x: ACID is a set of four important properties used to describe reliable transaction processing: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.
Atomicity means a transaction is treated as all-or-nothing. Either all of its required operations take effect, or none of its uncommitted effects remain after rollback or recovery.

x: a bank transfer should not permanently debit the sender without crediting the recipient.

b.x: Atomicity is supported by mechanisms such as transaction logs, undo information, rollback, and recovery procedures.
Atomicity does not mean that each individual SQL statement is physically executed at the exact same instant. It means the DBMS presents the transaction as a single logical unit.
Consistency means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another valid state, preserving the integrity rules that apply to the transaction.

x: A primary key must be unique and not null.
A foreign key must refer to a valid referenced row, subject to the DBMS's constraint rules.
A balance may be required to be non-negative.
A grade must be within an allowed range.
Business rules may require a transfer to preserve the total amount of money across the two accounts.

b.x: The DBMS can enforce some rules using constraints. Other business rules may require transaction logic or application checks.
Consistency does not mean that the database never changes. It means changes must respect the defined correctness rules.
Isolation concerns the interaction of concurrent transactions. Each transaction should be protected from inappropriate interference by other transactions.

The strongest familiar isolation model is serializable execution, where the result is equivalent to some serial ordering of transactions. Many systems also offer weaker isolation levels that allow particular anomalies in exchange for greater concurrency.
Isolation is commonly supported by locking, multiversion concurrency control (MVCC), timestamp ordering, or combinations of methods.
Durability means that once a transaction is successfully committed, its effects survive failures covered by the DBMS's durability guarantees.

x: Flushing log records to stable storage.
Replication and backups as additional availability measures.

b.x: A successful COMMIT is not the same as having a separate backup. Durability protects committed transactions within the system's failure model; backups help recover from other events such as accidental deletion, storage loss, or broader disasters.

x: both debit and credit occur, or neither transaction change remains.
account rules and the expected total are preserved.
concurrent transactions do not create an invalid result, such as spending the same available funds twice under the applicable isolation rules.
after commit, the new balances remain available after a covered crash and recovery.

b.x: Final balances after a successful transfer

x: Atomicity | Did all transaction operations happen as one unit? | Undo, rollback, recovery
Consistency | Were integrity rules preserved? | Constraints, application logic, correct transactions
Isolation | Did concurrent transactions interfere incorrectly? | Locks, MVCC, serializable scheduling
Durability | Do committed changes survive covered failures? | Logs, stable storage, redo, recovery

sec.s: A transaction may pass through several states:

b.x: A transaction may pass through several states:
The transaction is executing its read and write operations.
The final statement has executed, but the system may still need to make the commit durable.
The transaction has completed successfully and its changes are accepted as committed.
The transaction cannot continue because of an error, crash, constraint violation, deadlock victim selection, or another failure.
The transaction's uncommitted effects have been rolled back. It may be restarted if appropriate.
The transaction has left the system after completion or abort processing.
Active or Partially Committed → Failed → Aborted → Terminated or Restarted
Database theory often represents transaction actions as

x: T1: read(A), A = A - 100, write(A), commit

b.x: A schedule is the order in which operations from one or more transactions are executed. A serial schedule runs one transaction completely before another starts. A concurrent schedule interleaves operations from multiple transactions.
Concurrency can improve performance and resource utilization, but the DBMS must ensure that the interleaving is safe.
Two transactions read the same old value and both calculate updates. One update overwrites the other, so one logical change is lost.
A transaction reads data written by another transaction that has not committed. If the writer rolls back, the reader has used a value that never became committed data.
A transaction reads a row twice and sees different committed values because another transaction updated the row between reads.
A transaction repeats a query over a range and finds a different set of rows because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching the condition.
A transaction calculates an aggregate while another transaction updates several related records, causing the aggregate to combine values from inconsistent points in time.
Isolation levels and concurrency-control mechanisms determine which of these effects are permitted or prevented. The exact behavior can vary by DBMS and implementation.

sec.s: Concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transactions so that their combined execution preserves…

b.x: Concurrency control coordinates simultaneous transactions so that their combined execution preserves required correctness properties. It tries to balance correctness with throughput and response time.
Without concurrency control, users could overwrite one another's work, observe uncommitted data, or calculate results from inconsistent values.
A schedule is serializable if its effect is equivalent to a serial schedule of the same transactions.
Conflict serializability is a common test based on pairs of operations that:
Read-read operations on the same item do not conflict in the basic conflict-serializability test.

x: Create one node for each transaction.
For every conflicting pair, add a directed edge from the transaction whose operation occurs first to the transaction whose operation occurs later.
If the graph is acyclic, the schedule is conflict-serializable.
If the graph contains a directed cycle, it is not conflict-serializable.
T1 writes A before T2 reads A, so add T1 → T2.
If another conflict gives T2 → T1, the graph contains a cycle and the schedule is not conflict-serializable.

b.x: Transactions acquire locks before accessing data.
Each transaction receives a timestamp, and the system orders conflicting operations according to timestamp rules.
Transactions proceed with limited interference during a working phase and are validated before commit. Conflicts may cause a transaction to restart.

The DBMS keeps multiple versions of data so readers can often access a consistent snapshot without blocking writers in the same way as simple read locks. MVCC still needs rules for write conflicts and isolation guarantees.
This syllabus emphasizes lock-based protocols and deadlock handling, but understanding the other approaches gives context.

sec.s: A lock is a concurrency-control mechanism that restricts which operations may access a data item at a…

b.x: A lock is a concurrency-control mechanism that restricts which operations may access a data item at a particular time.
Before reading or writing an item, a transaction may need to obtain the appropriate lock. If another transaction holds an incompatible lock, the request may have to wait.
Locks may apply at different granularities
Coarse locks are simpler but may reduce concurrency. Fine-grained locks allow more transactions to proceed independently but can require more lock-management overhead.
Used for reading in a traditional lock model. Multiple transactions can generally hold shared locks on the same item at the same time.
Used for writing. An exclusive lock prevents other transactions from holding conflicting shared or exclusive locks on that item.
A transaction that reads X may request S-lock(X). A transaction that updates X generally needs an X-lock(X), sometimes by upgrading a prior S lock.
T1 needs to read a product price. It acquires S-lock(Price).
T2 also needs to read the price. It can normally acquire S-lock(Price).
T3 wants to change the price. It requests X-lock(Price), but must wait while the incompatible shared locks remain held.
This prevents T3 from changing the value in a way that interferes with the protected reads under the protocol.
The lock manager keeps track of

x: Whether a requested lock is compatible with existing locks.
Which waiting transaction can be granted a lock next.

b.x: When a transaction finishes or releases a lock, the lock manager may grant a waiting request.

A transaction may request an upgrade from S to X when it first reads an item and later needs to update it. If multiple transactions hold shared locks and all attempt to upgrade, they may block each other. Some DBMSs support lock conversion and specific policies to manage this situation.

sec.s: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) divides a transaction's locking behavior into two phases:

b.x: Two-Phase Locking (2PL) divides a transaction's locking behavior into two phases:
The transaction may acquire locks but does not release locks.
The transaction may release locks but does not acquire new locks.
Once a transaction releases its first lock, it cannot acquire additional locks under basic 2PL.

The basic 2PL protocol guarantees conflict serializability. However, it does not automatically prevent deadlocks, and a schedule may still require recovery from cascading aborts unless a stricter variant is used.
A transaction needs to update A and B.
A safe basic 2PL pattern may be

x: Read and update A and B.
Release locks when entering the shrinking phase.

b.x: After releasing a lock, it must not obtain a new lock under basic 2PL.

Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until the transaction commits or aborts. Many descriptions of strict 2PL also discuss retaining locks needed to prevent other transactions from reading uncommitted writes.

Strict 2PL prevents other transactions from reading or overwriting a value written by an uncommitted transaction when the required write locks are held until completion. It simplifies recovery and prevents cascading aborts due to reading uncommitted writes.
Rigorous 2PL holds all locks, including shared and exclusive locks, until commit or abort.
It is stricter than strict 2PL in common textbook terminology. The exact naming of variants can differ between textbooks, so state the locking rule clearly in an exam answer.
Conservative 2PL requires a transaction to obtain all locks it will need before it begins execution. If it cannot acquire them all, it waits without holding a partial set.

This prevents deadlocks caused by transactions holding some locks while waiting for others, provided the required lock set is known correctly in advance. The trade-off is reduced concurrency and the practical difficulty of knowing every required lock ahead of time.

x: Basic 2PL | Acquire locks, then release; no new locks after first release | Conflict serializability | Deadlocks possible
Strict 2PL | Hold write/exclusive locks until completion | Easier recovery; prevents dirty reads of uncommitted writes under the protocol | Deadlocks possible
Rigorous 2PL | Hold all locks until completion | Strong, straightforward ordering behavior | Can reduce concurrency
Conservative 2PL | Obtain all needed locks before starting | Avoids hold-and-wait deadlocks if lock set is known | May delay transactions; less concurrency

b.x: A DBMS may lock an entire table or individual rows. Row locks generally permit more concurrent work, but they create more lock-management overhead. Table locks are simpler but can block unrelated operations.

Intention locks signal that a transaction plans to acquire locks at a lower level in a hierarchy, such as row locks inside a table. They help the lock manager coordinate table-level and row-level requests without checking every row lock individually.

Lock escalation means replacing many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock, such as converting many row locks into a table lock. It can reduce lock-management overhead but may reduce concurrency. Whether and how escalation occurs depends on the DBMS.

sec.t: Deadlocks: Detection, Prevention, Avoidance, and Recovery
sec.s: A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are waiting indefinitely for resources held by one…

b.x: A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions are waiting indefinitely for resources held by one another, so none can make progress without intervention.

x: • T1 holds X-lock(A) and requests X-lock(B).
• T2 holds X-lock(B) and requests X-lock(A).

b.x: T1 waits for B, held by T2. T2 waits for A, held by T1. Neither can continue.
The classic four necessary conditions are:
At least one resource cannot be shared freely; only one transaction can hold the incompatible lock.
A transaction holds one or more resources while waiting for another.
Resources cannot simply be taken away arbitrarily; they are normally released by the holding transaction or through a controlled abort.
There is a cycle of transactions, each waiting for a resource held by the next.

A deadlock requires all four conditions in the classic model. Breaking one condition can prevent deadlocks, though practical systems often use detection and recovery rather than eliminating every condition.
A wait-for graph represents waiting relationships

x: An edge Ti → Tj means Ti is waiting for a resource held by Tj.

b.x: If the graph contains a directed cycle, a deadlock exists in the standard single-instance lock model.

For resource models with multiple instances and more complex resource types, detection can require additional analysis; the simple cycle rule is most directly applicable to transaction lock wait-for graphs.
The DBMS periodically or when needed builds or checks the wait-for graph. If a cycle is found, it selects a victim transaction to abort or roll back.

x: How much work the transaction has already completed.
Number and type of locks held.
How often a transaction has already been selected as a victim.

b.x: The objective is to break the cycle with minimal overall cost and avoid repeatedly sacrificing the same transaction.
Prevention schemes make at least one necessary deadlock condition impossible or impose rules that prevent cycles.

Require transactions to request resources in a global order. For example, every transaction must lock Account A before Account B if A sorts before B. Consistent ordering prevents circular wait when followed correctly.
Obtain all locks before execution, avoiding hold-and-wait.
The system may force a transaction to release resources by rolling it back under a defined policy.
Older and younger transactions receive different wait/rollback rules. Common textbook methods include wait-die and wound-wait.
Each transaction has a timestamp. Older transactions have smaller timestamps.

x: If an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger transaction, the older transaction is allowed to wait.
If a younger transaction requests a lock held by an older transaction, the younger transaction aborts (“dies”) and may restart with its original timestamp.

b.x: This policy is non-preemptive with respect to the lock holder. It prevents cycles by restricting which age relationships can wait.
Wound-wait uses the opposite style of rule

x: If an older transaction requests a resource held by a younger transaction, the younger transaction is rolled back (“wounded”).
If a younger transaction requests a resource held by an older transaction, the younger transaction waits.

b.x: The consistent timestamp ordering prevents circular waiting. A restarted transaction often retains its original timestamp so that it does not remain permanently disadvantaged.
Avoidance considers whether granting a request could lead the system into an unsafe state. In the general resource-allocation model, the Banker's algorithm is a classic example.
In database locking, complete knowledge of future lock requirements is often unavailable, so full avoidance may be impractical. Many DBMSs use detection and recovery, timeouts, or hybrid approaches.
If a transaction waits longer than a configured period, the DBMS may cancel it or treat it as a possible deadlock victim.

x: A long wait does not always mean a deadlock.
A timeout may abort a transaction that would soon have progressed.
A short timeout may cause unnecessary restarts.
Detect a deadlock or decide that a timeout policy has triggered.
Choose one transaction as a victim.
Roll back the victim fully or to a savepoint if supported and safe.
Allow the other transactions to continue.

b.x: The DBMS must avoid starvation, where a transaction is repeatedly selected as the victim and never completes. Policies may increase a transaction's priority after each rollback or account for how often it has been aborted.
A group of transactions is stuck in a circular wait.
One transaction waits or is repeatedly delayed for an unacceptably long time while other transactions continue to progress.
Deadlock is a circular dependency problem. Starvation is an unfairness or scheduling problem. A system can avoid deadlocks and still suffer starvation.

sec.s: Crash recovery is the process by which a DBMS restores the database to a correct state after a failure,…

b.x: Crash recovery is the process by which a DBMS restores the database to a correct state after a failure, such as:

x: A storage or I/O error within the recovery model.

b.x: A crash may occur while a transaction is running or just after a commit. Some changed pages may have reached storage while others have not. The DBMS must distinguish committed work from incomplete work.
A single transaction fails because of a constraint violation, application error, deadlock victim selection, or explicit rollback.
The database process or operating system stops unexpectedly. Volatile memory may be lost, while storage is assumed to remain intact under the basic crash model.
Storage containing database files is damaged or lost. Recovery may require backups, archived logs, replicas, or other copies.

In distributed systems, network or node failures can interrupt a transaction across multiple components. Such failures may require distributed commit and recovery protocols beyond the basic single-database crash model.
Volatile storage, such as ordinary RAM, loses its contents when power is lost.

Non-volatile storage, such as persistent storage devices, retains data across a power loss within the device's stated guarantees. Actual durability also depends on device behavior, controller caches, operating-system flushes, and correct configuration.
A DBMS uses logs and storage protocols to ensure that recovery can reconstruct the intended committed state.
After a crash, the DBMS aims to

x: Remove or compensate for incomplete transactions.
Ensure that data pages and transaction metadata agree.

sec.s: A transaction log is a record of important database actions used to recover after failures.

b.x: A transaction log is a record of important database actions used to recover after failures. A log may contain entries such as:

x: Old and new values, or information sufficient to undo/redo the change.

b.x: The exact log format is DBMS-specific.
This is only a teaching example; production logs use specific page, record, transaction, and recovery metadata.
Write-ahead logging is a central recovery principle.

The essential idea is that the log information needed to recover a change must be written to stable storage before the corresponding changed data page is allowed to be written to its permanent database location.

For commit durability, the DBMS also needs to ensure that the transaction's commit record and required preceding log records have reached stable storage according to its durability policy before it reports successful commit.

x: Then allow affected data pages to be written as required.
On recovery, use the log to undo or redo work.

b.x: Exact ordering and flushing rules depend on the DBMS and storage configuration.
Undo information allows the DBMS to reverse the effects of an incomplete transaction.
Redo information allows the DBMS to reapply a change that belongs in the recovered database but may not have reached the data files before the crash.
A log might store old and new values
The old value can support undo, while the new value can support redo, assuming the DBMS's recovery design records and interprets such information.

A checkpoint records recovery-related information that helps limit how much of the log must be examined after a crash. Depending on the DBMS, a checkpoint may record active transactions, dirty pages, log sequence information, or related metadata.

Without checkpoints, recovery might need to inspect a much longer log history. With checkpoints, the system can often start from a more recent recovery point, although it may still need to process log records before or after the checkpoint depending on the recovery algorithm.
A checkpoint is not necessarily a full backup and does not automatically mean every data page has been flushed to disk. The meaning of a checkpoint is specific to the DBMS's implementation.

x: Which changes may need to be undone.
Which committed changes may need to be redone.

sec.s: Undo reverses the effects of transactions that did not commit before the crash, according to the recovery…

b.x: Undo reverses the effects of transactions that did not commit before the crash, according to the recovery algorithm.

x: T1 changes A from 100 to 80 but crashes before commit. If the change reached a data page, recovery uses undo information to restore A to 100.

b.x: Undo is associated with atomicity: incomplete transactions should not leave permanent partial effects.
Redo reapplies changes that should be present in the recovered database but may not have been written to the data files before the crash.

x: T2 changes A from 100 to 80 and commits. The commit record reaches stable storage, but the changed data page does not reach its final location before the crash. Recovery can redo the committed change so A becomes 80.

b.x: Many recovery designs use both undo and redo

x: Undo effects of transactions that were incomplete at the time of the crash.
Redo effects of committed transactions whose changes may not yet be reflected in data pages.

b.x: The exact algorithm depends on logging policy, page-flushing rules, and the DBMS.
Database pages are not updated with a transaction's changes until after the transaction commits. This model can simplify recovery and often emphasizes redo.
Database pages may be updated before the transaction commits. The log must contain enough information to undo uncommitted changes and may also need redo information.
Real DBMS recovery is more sophisticated than these simplified categories, but the distinction helps explain why undo and redo information are needed.
A crash happens after the final log record.
T1 committed. If its change to A was not reflected in the database page, recovery may redo the change so A becomes 80.
T2 did not commit. If its change to B reached the database page, recovery may undo it so B returns to 50.
The final recovered state should include T1's committed result and exclude T2's incomplete result.

A DBMS recovery manager coordinates logging, checkpoints, undo, redo, and restart. Its responsibilities include ensuring that transaction outcomes remain correct after crashes and coordinating with the buffer manager and storage layer.

sec.s: Availability means the database service is accessible when users need it.

b.x: Availability means the database service is accessible when users need it. Crash recovery contributes to availability by helping the database restart in a consistent state after a failure.
Recovery alone does not guarantee high availability. If a storage device is destroyed, the database may need restoration from backups or failover to a replica.
A backup is a separate copy of database data used to recover from data loss, corruption, accidental deletion, or media failure.

x: Full backup: a copy of the database at a point in time.
Incremental backup: captures changes since a previous backup or backup point, depending on the system.
Differential backup: captures changes since a specified full backup, in systems that support this approach.
Logical backup: exports database objects and data in a logical form.
Physical backup: copies database files or storage-level representations.

b.x: The exact backup types and restore procedures depend on the DBMS.
Point-in-time recovery restores a database to a particular time or transaction point, commonly by restoring a suitable backup and replaying archived or transaction logs up to the desired point.
This can help recover from accidental deletion or a faulty update, assuming suitable backups and logs exist.

Replication maintains copies of data on multiple servers or nodes. It can improve availability and sometimes performance, but replication is not a substitute for backups: accidental deletion or corrupted changes may be replicated to all copies.
The target maximum time an organization can tolerate a service being unavailable.
The target maximum amount of data loss measured in time that the organization can tolerate.

x: If RTO is 30 minutes, the goal is to restore service within 30 minutes after the defined failure. If RPO is 5 minutes, the goal is to limit lost updates to no more than about five minutes of data under the recovery plan.

b.x: These are planning targets, not guarantees by themselves. Meeting them requires appropriate backups, logs, infrastructure, testing, and operational procedures.
A backup is useful only if it can be restored. Organizations should test:

After a crash, a database should not become available by simply exposing a partially applied transaction. It must first complete required recovery work so that committed and incomplete transactions are handled correctly. Safe recovery protects correctness while enabling service to resume.

StudentName and SubjectName depend on only part of the composite key. If they are non-prime attributes, the relation violates 2NF.
EmployeeID is the key. DeptName depends on DeptID, which depends on EmployeeID. DeptID is not a superkey in EMPLOYEE and DeptName is non-prime, so the relation violates 3NF.
Suppose a relation R(A, B, C) has

x: AB determines C and therefore all attributes.
AC determines B through C → B, so AC also determines all attributes.

b.x: Thus AB and AC are candidate keys. B and C are prime attributes because they belong to candidate keys. The dependency C → B may satisfy 3NF because B is prime, but C is not a superkey, so it violates BCNF.

x: the related database updates should not leave a half-created order if the transaction fails.
inventory, foreign keys, quantities, and order-state rules must remain valid.
concurrent orders should not oversell inventory under the selected concurrency rules.
after successful commit, the order and related changes should survive the failures covered by the system's guarantees.

b.x: Real payment systems often interact with external payment providers. A database transaction cannot automatically roll back an external card charge. Such systems may require idempotency, payment authorization/capture workflows, compensating actions, and distributed coordination.
T1 holds X-lock(A) and requests X-lock(B).
T2 holds X-lock(B) and requests X-lock(A).
The cycle shows a deadlock. The DBMS can abort one transaction, release its locks, and allow the other to continue.

T1 committed, so its change should appear after recovery. T2 did not commit, so its uncommitted change should not remain. The recovery manager uses the log and storage state to redo and/or undo as required.

sec.s: The following examples use broadly familiar SQL syntax.

b.x: The following examples use broadly familiar SQL syntax. Transaction behavior and supported syntax vary across database products. SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle have differences, so consult the relevant DBMS documentation for production code.

The design separates student, department, course, and enrolment facts. The composite primary key in Enrolment prevents the same student-course pair from being entered more than once, assuming that rule matches the business requirements.
If a required operation fails before commit, use ROLLBACK when appropriate. A production application should handle errors and verify that the expected row was updated.
If the DBMS supports this transaction pattern and the update was uncommitted, the change is cancelled.
The CHECK constraint helps enforce a non-negative balance at the row level. More complex multi-row rules may require other mechanisms and careful concurrency handling.

A foreign key can prevent a student record from referencing a department that does not exist, subject to the DBMS's configuration and constraint rules. For example, SQLite applications should ensure foreign-key enforcement is enabled for the connection when required.

Do not assume that every SQL statement is automatically part of one atomic multi-statement transaction. Explicitly understand transaction boundaries in the chosen DBMS and application driver. Avoid reporting success to the user until the commit has succeeded.

sec.s: Quick reference sheet

b.x: A non-prime attribute depends on only part of a composite candidate key. It is relevant to 2NF.
A non-prime attribute depends on a key through an intermediate non-superkey determinant in common textbook examples. It is relevant to 3NF.

x: For every non-trivial FD X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime.
For every non-trivial FD X → Y, X must be a superkey.

b.x: Therefore BCNF is stricter. Every BCNF relation satisfies 3NF, but not every 3NF relation satisfies BCNF.
An incomplete transaction does not leave a partial committed effect.
A successfully committed transaction's effects survive failures covered by the system's guarantees.
Transactions preserve integrity constraints and business rules.
Concurrent transactions are coordinated so their interactions obey the chosen isolation guarantee.
Transactions wait on each other's locks. The database process may still be running, and recovery may involve aborting a victim transaction.
The system or database process stops unexpectedly. Restart recovery uses persistent logs and other recovery information.
Reverse changes that should not remain, typically from incomplete transactions.
Reapply changes that should remain, typically committed changes that may not have reached data pages.

x: Detection and recovery | Find cycles and abort a victim | Work is wasted when a transaction is rolled back
Prevention | Make a necessary deadlock condition impossible | May reduce concurrency
Avoidance | Grant requests only when the resulting state is safe | May need knowledge of future resource requirements
Timeout | Cancel transactions that wait too long | May confuse a long wait with a deadlock
Transaction log | Records changes and transaction outcomes
Write-ahead logging | Ensures required log records are persisted before relevant data-page writes
Checkpoint | Helps reduce restart recovery work
Undo | Removes effects of incomplete transactions
Redo | Reapplies changes that should be present
Backup | Provides a separate copy for recovery from data loss
Replication | Maintains copies to support availability or distribution

b.x: The central lesson is that good database design and reliable transaction processing work together. Normalization structures data so that facts are stored consistently. ACID transactions and concurrency-control protocols keep simultaneous changes correct. Logging, checkpoints, and recovery procedures help the DBMS restore a consistent state after a failure. A dependable database requires all of these ideas to work together.
